proof:
# Two nested convex level sets do not imply the sharp continuous depth constant

Let

    T=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)},
    A=conv{(0,0),(4/5,0),(0,8/25)}⊂T,
    f=1_T+(1/256)1_A.

The nonzero superlevel sets of f are exactly T and A (with possible
empty level sets). Hence f is quasi-concave in the standard sense.
Its integral is

    M=|T|+|A|/256=1/2+(16/125)/256=1001/2000.

Nevertheless the maximum normalized halfspace depth of the measure
f(x)dx, even allowing the center anywhere in the entire plane, is
strictly smaller than γ_2=4/9.

## Three closed caps

Put

    e=1/1000,
    a=1/3−e/16=15997/48000,
    b=1/3−41e/125=124877/375000.

Consider H_1={x≥a}, H_2={y≥b}, and H_3={x+y≤a+b}.
These closed halfplanes cover R²: outside the first two, x<a and y<b,
so x+y<a+b. All boundary points are included in the cover.

For uniform mass on T, the respective fractions are(1−a)²,(1−b)²,
and(a+b)². The additional mass on A is e times |T|. Its three cap
fractions are

    (1−5a/4)²,        0,
    1−(5/3)(1−5(a+b)/4)².

Indeed b>8/25, so the second cap misses A. For the first cap use a
similar triangle. For the third, the linear form(x+y)/(4/5) takes
vertex values0,1,2/5 on A. Its upper tail at any v∈[2/5,1] is
(1−v)²/(1−2/5). Here v=5(a+b)/4 is in that interval.

Thus the three cap masses divided by |T| are

    U_1=(1−a)²+e(1−5a/4)²,
    U_2=(1−b)²,
    U_3=(a+b)²+e[1−(5/3)(1−5(a+b)/4)²].

Their exact positive deficits below(4/9)M/|T|=1001/2250 are

    1001/2250−U_1=3397759/163840000000,
    1001/2250−U_2=984871/140625000000,
    1001/2250−U_3=159342264433/13824000000000000.

Every point belongs to at least one of these closed caps, and every
one has mass strictly less than(4/9)M. This proves the claim.
The density is absolutely continuous, so the boundaries carry no mass;
the proof nevertheless uses closed caps throughout.

This is an auxiliary counterexample to a quasi-concave-density
statement. It is not a counterexample to any mixed-integer theorem.
In particular it does not establish that this two-level density can
be realized with the specific ordered weights and compatibility
constraints of a mixed-fiber ray shadow.
